name: Socrates
majorWorks: Wrote nothing himself; known through Plato's dialogues and Xenophon
centralQuestions: How should one live?
What is virtue, and can it be taught?

keyConcepts.definition: Reaching clarity by relentlessly questioning claims and definitions rather than asserting doctrine.
Cross-examination that exposes contradictions in a person's stated beliefs.
A state of productive puzzlement reached when confident beliefs turn out to be confused.

majorArguments: Claimed his only wisdom was knowing that he did not know — genuine inquiry starts by admitting ignorance.
Argued that no one knowingly does wrong; wrongdoing comes from mistaken beliefs about what is good.
frame: asks you to define your terms precisely, then tests that definition against hard cases until it either survives or breaks
context: Athens during its democratic and imperial peak, followed by defeat in the Peloponnesian War; Socrates was tried and executed for 'corrupting the youth' and impiety.
criticisms: We only know him through others' writings, so it's unclear how much is Socrates and how much is Plato's invention.
His method is better at dismantling bad definitions than building positive knowledge.
relevance: The template for treating a conversation partner's confidence as a starting point for inquiry, not a conclusion.
secondarySources: Gregory Vlastos, Socrates: Ironist and Moral Philosopher

name: Plato
centralQuestions: What is justice?
What is truly real, behind changing appearances?

keyConcepts.definition: Perfect, unchanging templates (Justice, Beauty) that particular things only imperfectly reflect.
Reason, spirit, and appetite, whose right ordering constitutes personal justice.
The idea that political rule should belong to those who understand the Good, not those who merely want power.

majorArguments: In the Allegory of the Cave, argued most people mistake shadows for reality and that philosophy is the difficult ascent toward truth.
Argued that justice in a person mirrors justice in a city: both require reason governing the other parts well.
frame: asks you to distinguish the appearance of a thing from its true, stable Form, and treats reasoned knowledge as categorically different from opinion
context: Wrote in the aftermath of Athens's defeat and Socrates's execution, deeply distrustful of democratic opinion as a guide to truth or justice.
criticisms: The independent existence of abstract Forms is hard to verify or even coherently locate.
His ideal of rule by a reasoning elite sits uneasily with democratic and pluralistic values.
relevance: Still the reference point for any argument that draws a line between how things seem and how they really are.
secondarySources: Julia Annas, An Introduction to Plato's Republic

name: Aristotle
centralQuestions: What is the good life for a human being?
What makes something what it is?

keyConcepts.definition: Human flourishing achieved through virtuous activity over a full life, not a fleeting feeling.
Virtue as a balance between two extremes, e.g. courage between cowardice and recklessness.
The purpose or end toward which a thing's nature directs it.

majorArguments: Argued that virtue is built through habituation — we become just by repeatedly acting justly, not by grasping justice in the abstract.
Argued humans are naturally social ('political animals'), so flourishing is bound up with community, not achieved in isolation.
frame: asks what a thing's proper function or purpose is, and evaluates it by how well it fulfills that function through practiced habit
context: Studied under Plato for twenty years, later tutored Alexander the Great, and founded his own school, the Lyceum, grounding ethics in observation rather than pure abstraction.
criticisms: His account of human nature reflects the biases of his time, including his views on women and slavery.
Offers less clear-cut guidance in genuine moral dilemmas than rule-based ethical systems.
relevance: The basis of modern virtue ethics: asking not 'what rule applies' but 'what kind of person is this action making me?'
secondarySources: Jonathan Barnes, Aristotle: A Very Short Introduction

name: Epictetus
centralQuestions: What is actually within our control?
How do we stay at peace amid what we can't control?

keyConcepts.definition: The core Stoic distinction between what is 'up to us' (judgments, choices) and what is not (outcomes, others' actions).
The faculty of moral choice — the one thing genuinely ours, regardless of circumstance.

majorArguments: Argued that disturbance comes not from events but from our judgments about events — a view Stoics thought empowering, not fatalistic.
Argued that external goods (health, reputation, wealth) are 'preferred' but never necessary for a good life.
frame: asks whether a given worry concerns something genuinely within your control, and redirects effort there instead of toward outcomes
context: Born enslaved in Hierapolis, later freed; taught in Rome until philosophers were banished by Domitian, then founded a school in Nicopolis.
criticisms: The practice can tip into emotional suppression rather than healthy processing of feeling.
Risks passivity toward genuinely changeable injustice by over-emphasizing 'acceptance'.
relevance: The direct ancestor of modern stress-resilience and cognitive-reframing techniques.
secondarySources: A.A. Long, Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life

name: Al-Farabi
centralQuestions: What makes a political community truly virtuous?
How does reason relate to revelation?

keyConcepts.definition: A political community organized around the pursuit of genuine happiness through shared knowledge and virtue.
A universal source of intelligibility that the human mind connects with in acts of understanding.

majorArguments: Argued that political philosophy and prophetic religion aim at the same truths through different methods — reasoned demonstration versus imaginative persuasion.
Argued that a genuinely virtuous city requires a ruler who combines philosophical understanding with practical and rhetorical skill.
frame: asks whether an institution or belief is organized around genuine understanding of the good, or merely around persuasion and habit
influenced: later Islamic and Jewish political philosophy
context: Wrote during the Abbasid Caliphate's major translation movement, which brought Greek philosophy into sustained dialogue with Islamic thought.
criticisms: His ideal 'virtuous city' is highly abstract and gives little practical guidance for actual governance.
Later thinkers questioned how cleanly he could align Aristotelian reason with revealed religion.
relevance: A key bridge figure showing philosophy as a genuinely cross-civilizational conversation, not a Western-only inheritance.
secondarySources: Majid Fakhry, Al-Farabi, Founder of Islamic Neoplatonism

name: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
centralQuestions: What distinguishes necessary existence from contingent existence?
What is the relationship between soul and body?

keyConcepts.definition: The distinction between a being whose existence is self-sufficient and beings that depend on something else to exist.
A thought experiment suggesting self-awareness is immediate and independent of sensing one's own body.

majorArguments: Argued that a chain of contingent causes cannot explain itself and must terminate in a necessary existent.
Argued, via the Flying Man thought experiment, that self-awareness does not depend on perceiving any part of the body.
frame: asks whether something's existence is self-explanatory or depends on something further, tracing dependency back to what does not
context: A polymath physician and philosopher in the Persian intellectual world, whose medical and philosophical works were standard texts in both the Islamic world and medieval Europe for centuries.
criticisms: His metaphysical system is highly technical and was heavily contested by later thinkers like Al-Ghazali.
Critics argue the Flying Man argument proves less about the soul's independence than Avicenna claimed.
relevance: His causal argument for a necessary being remains a reference point in philosophy of religion.
secondarySources: Jon McGinnis, Avicenna

name: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
majorWorks: Teachings preserved orally, later compiled in the Pali Canon and other early collections
centralQuestions: Why do humans suffer, and how can suffering be released?
Is there a fixed, independent self?

keyConcepts.definition: Suffering exists, it has a cause (craving), it can cease, and there is a path to its cessation.
The claim that the sense of a fixed, separate 'I' is itself a construction worth examining, not a given.
All things, including the self, are in constant change.

majorArguments: Argued suffering arises from craving and attachment, often rooted in mistaking an ever-changing process for a fixed self.
Argued release from suffering comes through a practical path (the Eightfold Path), not through metaphysical speculation alone.
frame: asks what you are clinging to in this situation, and whether the thing you're calling 'yourself' is as fixed as it feels
influences: Vedic and Śramaṇa renunciant traditions of ancient India
context: Taught in the Ganges plain amid a flourishing of renunciant movements questioning Vedic ritualism, later diversifying into Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana traditions across Asia.
criticisms: Secular adaptations sometimes strip out the ethical and communal framework the practices were embedded in.
Traditions vary enormously; treating 'Buddhism' as one monolithic view can flatten real doctrinal disagreement.
relevance: Underpins contemporary mindfulness and offers a rigorous challenge to assuming the self is simple and fixed.
secondarySources: Walpola Rahula, What the Buddha Taught

name: Nagarjuna
majorWorks: Mulamadhyamakakarika (Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way)
centralQuestions: Do things have inherent, independent existence?
What is the 'middle way' between existence and non-existence?

keyConcepts.definition: The claim that things lack fixed, independent essence — they exist only relationally, dependent on other things.
Things arise in interdependence with other things, never in true isolation.

majorArguments: Argued that if things had truly independent, fixed essences, change and causation would be impossible — so emptiness is compatible with, not opposed to, a functioning world.
Used systematic logical analysis to show that neither 'things exist inherently' nor 'nothing exists at all' survives scrutiny.
frame: asks whether the thing under discussion has a fixed, independent essence, or whether it only exists in relation to other things
context: Working within the developing scholastic tradition of Buddhist philosophy in classical India, using rigorous logical argument rather than purely devotional teaching.
criticisms: Critics have long debated whether 'emptiness' collapses into nihilism despite Nagarjuna's explicit denial of that reading.
His dense, technical style has produced centuries of competing interpretations.
relevance: A rigorous historical example of philosophy using pure logical analysis to dissolve, rather than answer, a metaphysical question.
secondarySources: Jay Garfield, The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way

name: Adi Shankara
majorWorks: Commentaries on the Brahma Sutras, principal Upanishads, and Bhagavad Gita
centralQuestions: What is the relationship between the individual self and ultimate reality?
What counts as genuine knowledge versus appearance?

keyConcepts.definition: The single, ultimate, unchanging reality underlying the apparent multiplicity of the world.
The innermost self, which Shankara's Advaita (non-dual) school holds to be identical with Brahman.
The way ordinary appearances can obscure, rather than reveal, ultimate reality.

majorArguments: Argued, through systematic commentary, that apparent multiplicity and separateness are a matter of ignorance (avidya) rather than final truth.
Argued that liberation (moksha) comes through direct knowledge of the self's identity with Brahman, not merely ritual action.
frame: asks you to distinguish what is ultimately, unchangingly real from what only appears real from a limited vantage point
influenced: Advaita Vedanta as a living tradition
context: Traveled widely across India establishing monastic centers, consolidating Advaita Vedanta into a systematic philosophical school within a rich, contested field of Indian metaphysics.
criticisms: Rival Vedanta schools (Ramanuja's qualified non-dualism, Madhva's dualism) directly reject his reading of the same core texts.
Critics argue his framework can undervalue the reality and importance of everyday ethical and social life.
relevance: A central reference point for any 'non-dual' or 'the self is not separate' claim encountered in contemporary spirituality.
primarySources: Shankara, Commentary on the Brahma Sutras (selections)
secondarySources: Eliot Deutsch, Advaita Vedanta: A Philosophical Reconstruction

name: Confucius
centralQuestions: How should we cultivate ourselves and relate to others to create social harmony?

keyConcepts.definition: Genuine care for others, cultivated through practice rather than innate and automatic.
Social forms and etiquette that structure respectful relationships and hold society together.
Ruler–subject, parent–child, husband–wife, elder–younger sibling, and friend–friend, each carrying reciprocal duties.

majorArguments: Argued that moral and social order begins with self-cultivation expressed through proper, reciprocal relationships, not through law or force alone.
Argued that ritual, properly understood, is not empty formality but the practiced shape genuine care takes in a community.
frame: asks what a given relationship owes and is owed, and how ritual or habitual practice could shape better conduct over time
influenced: East Asian political and educational institutions for over two millennia
context: Taught during China's turbulent Warring States-adjacent period, proposing cultivated virtue and right relationship as the path to restoring social harmony.
criticisms: Traditional interpretations have been used to justify rigid hierarchy, including patriarchal family roles.
Its relational ethics can struggle to address obligations to strangers outside one's named relationships.
relevance: A major, non-Western alternative to individual-rights-first ethics: asking what a relationship requires rather than only what a person is owed.
secondarySources: Philip J. Ivanhoe, Confucian Moral Self Cultivation

name: Laozi
centralQuestions: How can we live in harmony with the natural order rather than against it?

keyConcepts.definition: The underlying flow of the universe, which resists being fully captured in words or fixed concepts.
'Non-forcing' or effortless action — acting in harmony with circumstances rather than against the grain.
Complementary opposites that generate each other rather than opposing in simple conflict.

majorArguments: Argued that forceful striving and rigid control often undermine the very outcomes they aim at, while yielding and adaptability often outlast them.
Argued that the Dao that can be fully named or defined is not the eternal Dao — some truths resist final conceptual capture.
frame: asks where you're forcing something that wants to flow, and what would happen if you yielded instead of pushing
context: Emerged in China alongside Confucianism, offering a naturalistic, often anti-authoritarian counterpoint to Confucian ritual and hierarchy.
criticisms: Its embrace of 'letting things be' can be read as fatalism or an excuse for inaction in the face of injustice.
The concept of the Dao is intentionally elusive, making the philosophy hard to pin down or apply consistently.
relevance: A recurring counterweight, across many traditions, to the assumption that more control and more effort are always better.
secondarySources: Chad Hansen, A Daoist Theory of Chinese Thought

name: Anton Wilhelm Amo
region: Born in present-day Ghana; educated and worked in Germany
majorWorks: On the Absence of Sensation in the Human Mind and Its Presence in Our Organic and Living Body
The Art of Philosophizing Soberly and Accurately
centralQuestions: Does the mind itself sense, or only the living body?
What method keeps philosophical reasoning rigorous?

keyConcepts.definition: Amo argued sensation belongs to the living, organic body, not to the immaterial mind directly.
A disciplined method for reasoning accurately and avoiding empty verbal disputes.

majorArguments: Argued against Cartesian-style views by holding that sensation is a bodily, not purely mental, phenomenon.
Argued philosophy needed methodological discipline to avoid mistaking confused language for genuine insight.
frame: asks you to locate precisely where a phenomenon actually occurs — in mind, in body, or in their interaction — rather than assuming
influences: German university philosophy of his era
influenced: Later scholarship on the history of Black European intellectual life; his work was largely erased for centuries and only recovered by modern historians of philosophy
context: Brought to Germany as a child, Amo earned doctorates and taught at German universities in the 1730s–40s — the first known African philosopher to hold a position in a European university, before eventually returning to West Africa.
criticisms: His original Latin texts remained obscure for centuries, so his direct influence on later philosophy was limited relative to his talent.
Some of his arguments follow Enlightenment rationalist assumptions that were later strongly contested.
relevance: A concrete correction to the myth that the Enlightenment academy was ethnically homogeneous, and a reminder of how selectively philosophical canons get built.
primarySources: Amo, On the Absence of Sensation in the Human Mind (trans. selections)
secondarySources: Justin E.H. Smith, 'Introduction' in Amo's Philosophical Dissertations

name: Kwasi Wiredu
centralQuestions: How can philosophy engage African concepts on their own terms rather than through borrowed Western categories?
What can African consensus-based decision-making teach political philosophy?

keyConcepts.definition: The project of examining inherited philosophical concepts for unexamined assumptions imported from colonial languages and categories.
Wiredu's account, drawn from traditional Akan governance, of decision-making by consensus-building rather than majority-rule alone.

majorArguments: Argued that translating African concepts directly into inherited European philosophical vocabulary can distort them, and that careful conceptual work is needed to recover what's actually being claimed.
Argued that Akan traditions of consensus-seeking governance offer a genuine alternative model to adversarial majority-rule democracy, not merely a historical curiosity.
frame: asks whether a concept under discussion is being examined on its own terms, or quietly forced into a framework borrowed from elsewhere
influenced: comparative political theory on consensus democracy
context: Trained in analytic philosophy in the UK, then returned to build African philosophy as a rigorous academic field engaging both indigenous traditions and global philosophical method.
criticisms: Critics debate how much of 'traditional' Akan governance he describes reflects idealized reconstruction versus documented historical practice.
Some argue his analytic method itself imports assumptions it claims to be decolonizing.
relevance: A leading model for taking non-Western political philosophy seriously as live theory, not only as historical anthropology.
primarySources: Wiredu, Philosophy and an African Culture
secondarySources: Olusegun Oladipo (ed.), The Third Way in African Philosophy

name: Vine Deloria Jr.
centralQuestions: How does grounding religious and political thought in land and place differ from time-centered Western frameworks?
What does genuine tribal sovereignty require?

keyConcepts.definition: Deloria's argument that many Indigenous traditions organize meaning around specific places, in contrast to Western traditions organized around historical time and progress.
Political self-determination understood through ongoing treaty relationships and responsibilities to land, not only through abstract rights language.

majorArguments: Argued that treating Indigenous religions as primitive precursors to Christianity misreads traditions that are philosophically coherent on their own, place-centered terms.
Argued federal Indian policy repeatedly substituted paternalistic assumptions for genuine engagement with tribal self-governance.
frame: asks whether a claim is being organized around a particular relationship to place, and challenges assumptions that progress-through-time is the only valid frame
influences: Standing Rock Sioux tradition and law
critical engagement with Western theology and political theory
influenced: critical legal studies on tribal sovereignty
context: Wrote during the Red Power movement and the rise of federal Indian self-determination policy, combining legal advocacy, theology, and philosophy.
criticisms: Some scholars argue his contrast between 'space-centered' and 'time-centered' traditions is broader than the historical evidence fully supports.
His sharp critique of Christian theology drew pushback from both Christian and secular scholars.
relevance: A central figure for taking Indigenous philosophy seriously as rigorous contemporary theory, not folklore or a closed historical chapter.
primarySources: Deloria, Custer Died for Your Sins
secondarySources: David E. Wilkins, 'Introduction' in Deloria's For This Land: Writings on Religion in America

name: René Descartes
centralQuestions: What can be known with absolute certainty?
What is the relationship between mind and body?

keyConcepts.definition: Deliberately doubting everything that can possibly be doubted, to find what survives as certain.
'I think, therefore I am' — the claim that the act of doubting proves the existence of a thinking self.
The view that mind and body are two fundamentally different kinds of substance.

majorArguments: Argued that even a deceiving demon fooling him about everything else could not fool him about the fact that he was thinking.
Argued the mind can be conceived clearly and distinctly apart from the body, suggesting they are genuinely separate substances.
frame: asks what remains standing after you doubt everything you possibly can — and builds back up only from what survives
influences: mathematics and the new science of his era
context: Wrote during the Scientific Revolution, seeking a foundation for knowledge that didn't depend on inherited Scholastic authority.
criticisms: Mind–body dualism struggles to explain how two totally different substances causally interact.
Critics argue the 'cogito' proves less than Descartes claimed — perhaps only that thinking is occurring, not that a persisting 'I' exists.
relevance: The starting point for nearly all subsequent debate over mind, certainty, and consciousness in Western philosophy.
secondarySources: Bernard Williams, Descartes: The Project of Pure Enquiry

name: John Locke
centralQuestions: Where does knowledge come from?
What justifies political authority and property?

keyConcepts.definition: The mind at birth as a 'blank slate,' with knowledge built entirely from experience.
Rights to life, liberty, and property that exist prior to and independent of government.
Government's legitimacy derives from the consent of the governed, who can withdraw that consent.

majorArguments: Argued all ideas ultimately derive from sensory experience, rejecting innate ideas as the source of knowledge.
Argued a government that violates the natural rights it exists to protect forfeits its legitimacy and can justly be resisted.
frame: asks what a person consented to, and whether an authority still serves the purpose that justified creating it in the first place
influences: English constitutional conflicts of his era
influenced: Rousseau and later social contract theory
context: Wrote amid England's Glorious Revolution, defending a government limited by the consent and rights of the governed against absolutist claims.
criticisms: His property theory has been criticized for providing philosophical cover for colonial land seizure.
Critics question whether 'tacit consent' to government is coherent, since most people never actively consent to anything.
relevance: The direct philosophical ancestor of modern liberal-democratic ideas about rights, consent, and limited government.
secondarySources: John Dunn, Locke: A Very Short Introduction

name: David Hume
centralQuestions: What justifies our belief in cause and effect?
Can reason alone determine what we ought to do?

keyConcepts.definition: Past regularities (the sun rising) never logically guarantee future ones — we assume it from habit, not proof.
Descriptive facts about how things are cannot, by logic alone, generate prescriptive claims about how things ought to be.
Hume's claim that reason serves our desires and sentiments rather than determining our ultimate ends.

majorArguments: Argued causation is never directly observed, only the constant conjunction of events, which habit leads us to interpret as necessary connection.
Argued moral judgments arise from sentiment, not pure reason, since reason alone cannot motivate action.
frame: asks what experience actually shows, as opposed to what habit or sentiment leads us to assume follows from it
influenced: Kant (who credited Hume with waking him from 'dogmatic slumber')
context: Wrote during the Scottish Enlightenment, applying the empirical method rigorously enough to unsettle assumptions empiricism itself usually took for granted.
criticisms: His skepticism about induction and causation can seem to undercut the very science he admired.
Some argue his moral sentimentalism struggles to explain disagreement across cultures with different sentiments.
relevance: The is–ought distinction remains a standard tool for checking whether an argument smuggled in a value claim from a factual one.
primarySources: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
secondarySources: Barry Stroud, Hume

name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
centralQuestions: How can people live together freely, rather than merely be ruled?
Does civilization corrupt natural human goodness?

keyConcepts.definition: The collective will aimed at the common good, distinct from the mere sum of individual private wills.
Rousseau's controversial claim that submitting to the general will can itself be a form of freedom.
Humans are naturally good but corrupted by artificial social inequality and dependence.

majorArguments: Argued legitimate political authority must rest on the general will of the people, not on inherited power or elite expertise.
Argued that private property and social comparison, not human nature itself, are the roots of destructive inequality.
frame: asks whether an arrangement reflects the genuine common good the community would choose for itself, or just the strongest private interests
influences: Locke and social contract theory (in reaction)
context: Wrote as Enlightenment optimism about reason and progress was intensifying, and his critique of inequality directly influenced revolutionary politics in France.
criticisms: The 'general will' has been criticized as vague enough to justify majority tyranny over dissenting individuals.
His idealized 'natural man' rests on speculative anthropology rather than historical evidence.
relevance: Central to any debate over whether real freedom requires more than simply being left alone by others.
secondarySources: Nicholas Dent, Rousseau

name: Immanuel Kant
majorWorks: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
centralQuestions: What can we know, and what are the limits of reason?
What makes an action morally right?

keyConcepts.definition: Act only according to a rule you could will to become a universal law for everyone.
Genuine freedom as rational self-legislation — giving yourself the moral law, not merely following desire.
The distinction between things as they appear to us and things as they are in themselves, which we can never fully know.

majorArguments: Argued moral worth comes from acting out of duty to a universalizable principle, not from the consequences an action happens to produce.
Argued the mind actively structures experience (space, time, causality) rather than passively receiving a ready-made world.
frame: asks whether the principle behind an action could be willed as a universal law for everyone, without contradiction
influences: rationalist and empiricist traditions he sought to reconcile
context: Wrote in Enlightenment Prussia, attempting to secure both the authority of science and the possibility of genuine moral freedom against skeptical challenges.
criticisms: Critics argue his ethics can produce rigid conclusions (e.g., that lying is never permissible) that conflict with strong moral intuitions.
His account of autonomy has been criticized as overly abstract, detached from emotion, relationship, and context.
relevance: The reference point for any argument that judges actions by principle rather than outcome.
primarySources: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
secondarySources: Christine Korsgaard, Creating the Kingdom of Ends

name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
majorWorks: Elements of the Philosophy of Right
centralQuestions: How does freedom become real in history and institutions?
How is consciousness shaped through recognition by others?

keyConcepts.definition: A pattern of development through thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, resolving contradictions at a higher level of understanding.
Self-consciousness develops only through being recognized by another self-consciousness.
Freedom made concrete through family, civil society, and the state, not just abstract individual rights.

majorArguments: Argued that freedom is not simply being left alone, but becomes real only through rational institutions and mutual recognition.
Argued history is the gradual, often conflict-driven unfolding of human freedom's self-understanding.
frame: asks how a concept has developed through conflict and resolution over time, rather than treating it as fixed from the start
context: Wrote as Napoleon reshaped Europe and Germany was working out its own path to modern statehood, seeking to show reason at work in historical change itself.
criticisms: His system has been accused of justifying whatever historically prevailed as rationally necessary.
His prose is notoriously dense, and interpreters still disagree sharply about what he actually claimed.
relevance: Central to any argument that a concept (freedom, selfhood, justice) can only be understood by tracing its historical development.
secondarySources: Frederick Beiser, Hegel

name: Karl Marx
centralQuestions: How do economic structures shape ideas, freedom, and social conflict?
What is required for genuine human freedom under industrial capitalism?

keyConcepts.definition: The view that a society's economic 'base' shapes its politics, law, and ideas, more than the reverse.
Workers becoming estranged from their own labor, its products, and their fellow humans under capitalist production.
History driven by conflict between groups with opposing relationships to the means of production.

majorArguments: Argued that freedom must be considered in relation to material and economic conditions, not treated as a purely abstract legal or political matter.
Argued capitalism systematically extracts surplus value from workers' labor, generating both enormous productivity and deep alienation.
frame: asks who benefits materially from an arrangement, and how the underlying economic structure shapes the ideas people take to be natural or neutral
influenced: the Frankfurt School and critical theory
context: Wrote during industrialization's most brutal early decades in Europe, analyzing capitalism's dynamics from exile in London.
criticisms: His predictions about capitalism's inevitable collapse and revolution have not materialized as he described.
Regimes claiming his legacy produced severe political repression, a legacy his defenders argue distorts his actual theory.
relevance: Still the standard reference for any argument connecting economic structure to political ideology and social conflict.
secondarySources: Jonathan Wolff, Why Read Marx Today?

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
centralQuestions: Where do our moral values actually come from, historically?
How should one live after the 'death of God' undermines inherited certainties?

keyConcepts.definition: Tracing how moral concepts like 'good' and 'evil' emerged from specific historical power relations, not eternal truths.
A fundamental drive toward growth, mastery, and self-overcoming underlying much human behavior.
Nietzsche's contrast between value systems that affirm strength and vitality versus those that valorize weakness out of resentment.

majorArguments: Argued conventional morality itself may constrain rather than liberate the individual, and should be examined for its hidden origins in resentment or power.
Argued that without inherited religious or metaphysical certainty, individuals face the task of creating their own values rather than discovering ready-made ones.
frame: asks where a value actually came from historically, and whether it affirms life and strength or masks weakness and resentment
context: Wrote as traditional religious authority was visibly eroding in 19th-century Europe, diagnosing what he saw coming next rather than mourning what was lost.
criticisms: His writing was later distorted and appropriated by Nazi ideology, despite his own explicit contempt for antisemitism and nationalism.
Critics argue his 'will to power' framework can shade into glorifying domination if read uncharitably.
relevance: The essential tool for asking where a 'self-evident' moral value actually came from, and whose interests it originally served.
primarySources: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality
secondarySources: Brian Leiter, Nietzsche on Morality

name: John Stuart Mill
centralQuestions: What makes an action morally right?
Where should the boundary lie between individual liberty and society's authority?

keyConcepts.definition: Seek the greatest well-being for the greatest number, weighing everyone's happiness equally.
Society may only restrict a person's liberty to prevent harm to others, not merely for their own good or to enforce convention.
Mill's distinction between intellectual/moral pleasures and merely bodily ones, arguing not all pleasures are equally valuable.

majorArguments: Argued that everyone's well-being counts equally, and that actions should be judged by their consequences for overall welfare.
Argued vigorously that free expression benefits society even when — especially when — the opinion expressed turns out to be wrong, because it sharpens true beliefs through contest.
frame: asks what the actual consequences for overall well-being are, and whether restricting someone's liberty here truly prevents harm to others
influences: Harriet Taylor Mill (a major intellectual partner and influence)
context: Wrote during Victorian Britain's debates over democratic expansion, censorship, and the proper limits of state and social power over the individual.
criticisms: Utilitarian calculation can seem to justify harming a minority if it maximizes aggregate welfare.
Critics question whether 'higher' and 'lower' pleasures can be ranked without smuggling in Mill's own class-inflected tastes.
relevance: The direct ancestor of most contemporary arguments for free speech and cost-benefit-based public policy.
secondarySources: Alan Ryan, J.S. Mill

name: Hannah Arendt
centralQuestions: What conditions make totalitarianism possible?
What is the relationship between truth, action, and political life?

keyConcepts.definition: Arendt's controversial argument that great atrocities can be carried out by ordinary people through thoughtless bureaucratic conformity, not only by monstrous fanatics.
The capacity to begin something genuinely new through action, which Arendt saw as central to political freedom.
The shared space of appearance and speech among equals, distinct from private and economic life, where political freedom is exercised.

majorArguments: Argued totalitarianism was made possible by mass loneliness and the destruction of genuine plurality and public space, not merely by a charismatic tyrant.
Argued that truth and factual reality are preconditions for political freedom, and that systematic lying corrodes the shared world politics depends on.
frame: asks what conditions of public life and truthfulness make a given action or institution possible or impossible in the first place
influences: the Greek polis as a political model
influenced: Contemporary political theory on totalitarianism, truth, and public life
context: Fled Nazi Germany as a Jewish refugee, and wrote her major work analyzing totalitarianism and political life from direct personal experience of its collapse.
criticisms: Her 'banality of evil' thesis about Eichmann was fiercely contested by historians who argued he was a more committed ideologue than she portrayed.
Critics argue her sharp public/private distinction undervalues how economic and domestic conditions shape political freedom.
relevance: Essential for questions about how democracies erode, and how truth and public discourse relate to political freedom.
secondarySources: Margaret Canovan, Hannah Arendt: A Reinterpretation of Her Political Thought

name: Simone de Beauvoir
centralQuestions: How is 'woman' constructed as 'Other' in society?
What does it mean to live an authentically free, ethical existence?

keyConcepts.term: 'One is not born, but becomes, a woman'
keyConcepts.definition: Gender as socially constructed and produced through lived experience, not a fixed biological destiny.
The way a dominant group defines itself as the norm and defines a subordinate group in relation to, and lesser than, that norm.
Freedom is always exercised within concrete social and bodily circumstances, not as pure abstract choice.

majorArguments: Argued that women have historically been defined as deviation from a male norm ('the Other'), rather than as autonomous subjects in their own right.
Argued genuine ethical existence requires willing not only one's own freedom but also the freedom of others, since human freedoms are interdependent.
frame: asks how a group or identity has been defined in relation to a dominant norm, rather than on its own independent terms
context: Wrote in postwar France as an equal intellectual partner within the existentialist circle around Sartre, applying existentialist method rigorously to the lived situation of women.
criticisms: Critics argue The Second Sex reflects a mid-century, largely Western, middle-class perspective not fully generalizable across cultures.
Some feminist theorists argue her framework still measures women's freedom against a male-centered standard of transcendence.
relevance: The foundational philosophical text connecting existentialist freedom to the analysis of gender and social construction.
secondarySources: Sonia Kruks, Simone de Beauvoir and the Politics of Ambiguity

name: John Rawls
centralQuestions: What principles of justice would free and equal people agree to if they didn't know their own place in society?

keyConcepts.definition: A hypothetical choice situation for designing a just society's basic rules.
Choosing society's rules without knowing your own race, class, talents, or position — to ensure fairness.
Inequalities are only justified if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.

majorArguments: Argued that principles chosen behind a 'veil of ignorance' would prioritize basic liberties for all and permit inequality only when it benefits the worst-off.
Argued justice as fairness could ground a stable, pluralistic society without requiring citizens to share one comprehensive moral or religious worldview.
frame: asks what rules you would choose for a society if you didn't know in advance which position within it you'd occupy
influenced: debates over distributive justice and welfare policy
context: Wrote during the postwar expansion of the American welfare state and civil rights movement, aiming to give liberal democracy a rigorous philosophical foundation.
criticisms: Libertarian critics (notably Nozick) argue the difference principle licenses excessive redistribution that violates individual entitlement.
Communitarian critics argue his 'unencumbered' choosers behind the veil of ignorance are an unrealistic model of actual social selves.
relevance: The default reference point in contemporary debates over what a fair distribution of resources and opportunity actually requires.
secondarySources: Samuel Freeman, Rawls

name: Amartya Sen
centralQuestions: What should we actually be measuring when we ask whether a society is just or people are flourishing?

keyConcepts.definition: Justice and development should be measured by people's real freedom to achieve valuable functionings — what they can actually do and be — not just income or resources.
Sen argues philosophy should focus on comparing realistic options to reduce injustice, rather than only theorizing one perfectly just society.

majorArguments: Argued that measuring welfare by income or resources alone misses how differently people can convert those resources into real freedom and functioning (due to disability, discrimination, or context).

Argued famines are caused less by absolute food shortages than by failures of entitlement and political accountability — notably, that famines essentially do not occur in functioning democracies with a free press.
frame: asks what real, usable freedom a person has to do and be what they value, not just what resources are formally available to them
influences: his own empirical research on famine and development economics
influenced: contemporary development economics and global justice theory
context: Drew on his own experience of the 1943 Bengal famine and later Nobel Prize-winning economics work to reshape how philosophers and policymakers define development and justice.
criticisms: Critics argue the capability approach is harder to operationalize into clear policy metrics than simpler measures like income.
Some philosophers argue Sen never specifies a definitive list of capabilities, leaving the framework productively — or frustratingly — open-ended.
relevance: Central to how contemporary global institutions define and measure development, poverty, and justice.
secondarySources: Martha Nussbaum, Creating Capabilities
